content.content: Launching skill: artifact-design

content.text:
Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page - what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in. Format is not part of this read: author HTML, and publish Markdown only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it - a Markdown publish keeps its filename as its title and takes almost none of the craft below, and is never a way to save time.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first - CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world - its materials, instruments, vernacular - is where distinctive choices come from. Whatever the treatment, carry at least one detail only this subject would have - its real units and scales, its document conventions, its terms of art - as content, not ornament; it costs a plain page nothing. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. Google Fonts is the one font host the Artifact CSP admits - link it directly (`<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=...&display=swap">`); a face from anywhere else must be inlined as a @font-face data URI or it falls back silently. Either way, declare a real fallback stack. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Load libraries, don't paste them.** When the page genuinely needs a library - React, a charting or highlighting package - load its UMD build from cdnjs (only the script - a library's stylesheet still has to be inlined) with one pinned `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/...">` placed before the inline script that uses its global, instead of inlining the library's source or hand-writing a stand-in; the Artifact tool's description lists the few other script hosts the CSP admits. The page's own CSS and JS, its images and its data ship with the page. Most pages need no library at all - reach for one only when it carries real weight.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject - the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states, not two: an explicit choice stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting stamps *nothing* - most viewers see the un-stamped document, where only `prefers-color-scheme` separates light from dark. Structure the CSS token-level for all three: the bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice beats a dark OS; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also wins in the other direction. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block - a color whose only definition sits behind `[data-theme]` never applies in the un-stamped state, and the page renders one theme's text on the other theme's ground. Two more rules keep each theme resolving as a set: the artifact composites over a ground the viewer paints in *its* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token - a transparent body silently borrows the host's ground; and every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never a literal that only works in one theme. Declare every token in the bare `:root` block before any media or `[data-theme]` block redefines it - a color that exists only inside one of those blocks is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first - don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme - then skip the media query and stamps entirely but still paint the background and every color explicitly, so the page holds on either host ground; make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content - tables, code, diagrams - gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Compose repeated things as one object.** Cards in a row, label/value pairs down a list, badges on siblings: same edges, baselines and inner padding from one to the next, and a recurring element sits in the same place on each. Let content set a container's height and pick a column count the items fill, so nothing stretches over dead space or sits alone in a row. Text that can outgrow its track wraps or scrolls in its own container; clipped text is a bug.

**Not everything is a card.** Border, fill, radius and shadow each say "separate object" - spend them by role, lifting the one thing that needs it, instead of one radius and one shadow stamped on every block, which flattens the hierarchy. Lead with big-number tiles only when those figures are the point of the page.

**Draw charts to the scale.** One scale places marks, ticks and labels, and every label names a value the chart reaches; chart text takes its color from the theme tokens so it reads in both themes; marks, labels and edges stay clear of one another and inside the drawing's bounds - in SVG, leave room in the viewBox for the outermost labels and give every drawn shape an explicit fill.

**Show the page at rest.** Everything meant to be read is visible once the page has loaded, without scrolling to trigger it - that first still frame is what a thumbnail, a shared link, and a skimming reader all get. A section may animate in, but from a visible resting state, never parked at `opacity: 0` waiting on an observer. Size a hero to what it holds, not to the viewport; a `100vh` opener pushes the page itself out of that first frame. A tool or app opens in a realistic working state - the user's real data where it exists, otherwise example rows, a loaded sample, a form someone plausibly filled, plainly marked as examples and never passed off as the user's own figures - so the first look shows what it does; an empty shell waiting for input shows nothing.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly - their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out - a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen - name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it - no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Name the page like a product, not a caption.** The `<title>` is the artifact's name in the gallery and the browser tab, and it sets the reader's first impression of care. Give the page a real name: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific to the subject - or, for a page that exists to answer one question, that question itself, which is then the page's name. Stop at the name - a title that carries its own explainer after a dash or colon reads as generated filler. The name must also identify the page among many: in the gallery it sits beside dozens of other artifacts, and a generic category label that could sit on any of them fails as a name just as surely as an appended explainer. When a candidate title pairs the name with a generic word - a greeting, a category, a page-type label - the name is the half to keep; a trim that drops the identity and keeps the generic word produces exactly the title that could sit on any page. And the rule removes explainers, it does not impose brevity: a multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished, and shortening it further only makes it generic. The one-sentence publish `description` is where the explanation belongs; the gallery shows it right under the title.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number - a pill, a chip, a severity stripe - so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan - a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4-6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles - a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

**Write, look once, publish.** Before publishing you may look at the rendered page once - one screenshot of the local file, or the Artifact tool's preview where it offers one - then one pass of edits for what it shows, without a second look. For a page that charts real numbers, take that look rather than skip it, and spend it on the chart. Don't build a test loop around your own file: no repeated screenshots, no pulling the script out to run it through node, no scripts that probe the DOM. That loop spends the session re-checking what a careful write already settled, while the user waits for a link. Then publish, check once any `window.claude` call the preview couldn't run, and stop: the live page is the review surface, and further polish is the user's to ask for. If the user reports something visibly broken - a clipped column, unreadable text, a control that does nothing - fix that and republish once.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world - headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

Independent verification · third-party opinion

Bonsai-27B Prefill Audit

Is profiling_gemm_27b.md a fair measurement, and can someone else reproduce it? Checked against the 48 raw simulator logs, the build and sweep scripts, the kernel source, the elaborated RTL config, and the 48 measurement binaries.

Subject profiling_gemm_27b.md, generated 2026-08-31 Audited 2026-09-02 Evidence 104 logs · 48 binaries · 8 scripts

01 — OPINIONVerdict

The measurement is fair. The four builds share one compile line and differ only in the three flags the document names; the "before" build is genuine upstream RVV code, not a straw man; the measured region is bracketed identically in both code paths; and all 48 legs ran once, in one pass, with no reruns. Every one of the 48 published cycle counts matches its log exactly, and every ratio, geometric mean and curve fit in the document reproduces. The residual bias that does exist runs against the author: the optimized builds pay a scalar activation quantizer that the baseline does not, so the published speedups are lower bounds, and the choice of geometric mean understates the model-wide result by 14%.

Reproducibility is partial. The 27B prefill half regenerates cell-exact from logs on disk. The 27B decode half — roughly half of every comparison the document makes — has no logs anywhere in the tree and no command that would produce them. Every aggregate row is typed by hand rather than emitted by the tool, and one of them is wrong by 23.6%. Nothing is version-pinned: no commit, no toolchain, no simulator build, no model hash, and the binaries were built from an uncommitted working tree.

A−
Fairness
Clean A/B, honest baseline, no selective reporting. Marked down for two undisclosed asymmetries, not for any rigged number.
C+
Reproducibility
Prefill tables regenerate exactly. Decode half unverifiable, aggregates hand-made, nothing pinned.
48/48
published cycle counts matched their log, to the digit
62
derived figures independently recomputed and confirmed
3
statements that are factually wrong
1
major evidence gap: the entire 27B decode column

02 — FAIRNESSWhich way does the bias point?

A speedup number can be flattered in a dozen quiet ways. Every one we tested for either was not there, or pushed the result down rather than up.

PASS
One compile line for all four builds
build.sh configures every variant with the same Release, -O3, -static, -march=rv64gv_zca_zcb_zcmp_zcmt_zicbop_zihintpause, ZVFH=OFF, OPENMP=OFF. Only GGML_CPU_REPACK, Q1_PREFETCH_DIST and GGML_RV_XANDESVDOT move, and only d4 appends _xandesvdot to the march string.
PASS
The baseline is real upstream, not a crippled build
GGML_CPU_REPACK=OFF removes nothing a Q1_0 tensor would otherwise get — the repack dispatcher has exactly one Q1_0 candidate, and llamafile sgemm (on in both arms) has no Q1_0 case at all. Pristine runs the vectorized ggml_vec_dot_q1_0_q8_0_vl256.
PASS
The measured region is the same region in both paths
The ROI opens at ggml-cpu.c:1744, before the extra-buffer dispatch, and closes after the compute on both branches — so each build counts its own activation quantization. The ANDESIM_ROI_CLEAR_DPREF experiment knob is absent from all 48 measurement binaries.
PASS
The optimizations physically executed
Disassembly finds 32 nds.vd4dots in each of the two d4 kernels and zero in the other three builds; in-kernel prefetch.r appears only in prefetch and d4. No silent fallback — which the repo's own check-vd4dots.sh notes has happened before.
PASS
No selective reporting
All 48 legs are fresh run lines in one pass, zero resumes, zero non-zero exits. The resume rule structurally cannot re-run a leg that already produced a number. The only retry anywhere in the evidence set re-ran two 4B pristine legs that timed out — i.e. it helped the "before".
BIAS−
The optimized builds pay an activation quantizer the baseline does not
Pristine quantizes activations with the RVV quantize_row_q8_0; all three repack builds run the pure-scalar ggml_quantize_mat_q8_0_4x1, with an out-of-line __roundf per element, inside the same ROI. That is 6–60% of every published d4 cycle count and under 0.5% of the matching pristine one. Equalize it and attn_v/attn_k go from 11.40x to roughly 24–29x. The published speedups are lower bounds.
BIAS−
The mean chosen is the conservative one
The geometric mean gives a 1024-row node the same vote as a 17408-row node. Cycle-weighted over the whole model the result is 20.8x, not the document's 18.15x. The harness even documents the choice: sweep.sh refuses to print a cycle-weighted ratio because it "reads like a per-node speedup without being one".
Two more checks, and the one bias that points the other way
BIAS−
Prefetch's 1.07x is a floor, not a ceiling
The core, caches and 2 MB L3 are Verilator-elaborated Andes RTL, but main memory behind the L3 is a flat 1-cycle TLM model (vsim_andesim/src/platform/simple_memory.hpp:40, unsigned latency = 1). The prefetch stage exists to hide miss latency and this machine has almost none to hide, so it is the one number that should grow on silicon. The document's own explanation of it appeals to latency the simulator does not model.
BIAS+
The upstream comparator uses 32 of the machine's 128 vector lanes
quants.c:493 pins the upstream kernel to vsetvl_e8m1(32) with a horizontal reduction every 32 elements. On VLEN 1024 the e8m1 VLMAX is 128, so 96 lanes idle. This is unmodified upstream and therefore the right "what does upstream get on this chip today" number — but a material share of 20.6x is a 32-lane algorithm on a 128-lane machine, and the same figure would be far smaller at VLEN 256. The repo documents this in a sibling file; this write-up neither states nor links it.
GAP
The one-time repack is excluded and never mentioned
The layout conversion runs at model load, outside the ROI, at roughly 18 scalar instructions per weight element — about 1.6–2.4 billion cycles for ffn_down, or 58–141x one measured matmul of the same tensor. Excluding it is legitimate: it is amortized, upstream does exactly the same through the same hook for q4_0/q4_K/q6_K, and break-even against upstream arrives after about 18–34 prompt tokens. But a reader is never told, and the ~3x model-load inflation is visible in the timestamps of the very logs shipped as evidence.

03 — SCALEWhat the evidence actually supports

The document never states a whole-model number. Built from its own per-node measurements, weighted by the real layer counts (48 SSM + 16 attention) and the LM head, it is higher than every headline the document does give.

Whole-model MUL_MAT, cycle-weighted497 nodes · 94.57 G → 4.55 G cycles · recomputed here
20.8×
Document's headlinegeometric mean over 10 optimizable nodes
18.15×
If the LM head had failed the 64-row gatethe case on Bonsai-4B and 8B — 151,669 rows, 151669 % 64 = 53
10.8×
0×10×20.8×

Bars are drawn to the same linear scale. The 20.8x figure is insensitive to how the LM head is charged — as a 4-token gemm, a 2-token gemv, a 1-token gemv, or omitted entirely, it spans only 20.33–20.76x. It still excludes all non-MUL_MAT work, so it is an upper bound on end-to-end prefill.

The gap from 18.15x decomposes cleanly: geometric to cycle-weighted over the same ten shapes is +13.3%, layer multiplicity +2.5%, including the un-repacked ssm_alpha/ssm_beta is −2.0%, and the LM head is +0.4%.

The third bar is the document's largest undisclosed risk. output.weight is [5120 × 248320] — 1.27 G weights, 4.96% of every matmul weight in the model, larger than three whole layers. It is MUL_MAT node #497 and was never measured. It clears the repack gate only because 248320 is divisible by 64. Had it failed, it would be 50.3% of the optimized budget and the model-wide result would drop to 10.77x. The document spends a paragraph on that exact sensitivity for two tensors worth 0.13% of a layer, and does not name the tensor where it matters 5,000 times more.

04 — DEFECTSWhat is actually wrong

Three statements are false and several are imprecise. None of them moves a measured cycle count; two of them move a published number, and one sends the reader after a fix that does not exist.

D1

The layer-7 LAYER row is wrong by 23.6% in two cells

Error

| | LAYER | | 372,244,480 | 1,380,604,045 | 241,152,929 | 225,336,152 | 66,024,863 |

True values: +repack is 195,052,238, not 241,152,929. +prefetch is 182,336,759, not 225,336,152. The other three cells in the same row are exact, and layer 6's equivalent row is correct in all four columns. The wrong values are not any subset-sum of the measured nodes, so they are stale, not an alternative aggregation.

Impact: no speedup, geometric mean or conclusion derives from this row — every ratio in the document is computed per node and all of them check out. But a reader who divides the row to sanity-check the layer gets 5.72x instead of the true 7.08x.

D2

The vector quantizer the document blames a build flag for does not exist

Error

Its vector twin is gated behind __riscv_zvfh, and the measurement build sets -DGGML_RV_ZVFH=OFF.

What is true: on RISC-V, arch-fallback.h:221 unconditionally aliases ggml_quantize_mat_q8_0_4x1_generic to ggml_quantize_mat_q8_0_4x1. Both arms of the #if defined(__riscv_zvfh) at repack.cpp:347-351 therefore call the same scalar function. There is no RISC-V vector implementation anywhere in the tree, and building with ZVFH=ON would change nothing.

Impact: no cycle count changes — prefill genuinely does run a scalar quantizer. What changes is the remedy. The document points the reader at a CMake option, implying the measurement handicapped itself and one flag recovers the loss. The real work is writing an RVV quantizer, which the author's own opt_roadmap.md correctly lists as unwritten code.

D3

Half of the 12.4x fixed-cost gap is just four tokens instead of two

Overstated

So decode gets a vector quantizer and prefill gets a scalar one. That is the whole 12.4x fixed-cost gap

What is true: 489,581/39,491 = 12.40x per call is correct, but the gemm call quantizes 4 token rows and the gemv call 2. Per token it is 122,395 vs 19,745 — 6.2x. The two Fs differ in routine and in workload; only the first is the scalar/vector choice.

Impact: the penalty attributed to the scalar quantizer halves. The conclusion survives — a 6.2x per-token penalty is still the largest single item in a small prefill matmul, and vectorizing it is still the best remaining prefill lever.

Four smaller inaccuracies, with corrections
D4
"F stays put" is contradicted by the table above it
gemv F goes 13,379 → 27,294 → 39,491 — a 2.95x rise the document prints itself. gemm F rises 23%. The point being made (F's share grows as T collapses) is true and worth making; the absolute claim is not.
D5
"0.06% of the layer's weights" — the true figure is 0.128%
The Notes bullet halves it, counting one tensor instead of two. Line 71 of the same document states it correctly as 0.12%. The companion figure in the same sentence, 2.7% of optimized cycles, is right (2.74%).
D6
"their four cycle counts agree to 0.3%" — only one of the two does
ssm_alpha's spread is 0.30%; ssm_beta's is 0.46%. Worth stating precisely, because these two tensors run bit-identical code in all four builds and are therefore the document's only measurement of its own noise floor.
D7
"Measuring one of each covers the whole model" — it omits the largest tensor
The LM head is 4.96% of all matmul weights and is measured nowhere. See section 03.

05 — REPRODUCTIONCan someone else get these numbers?

Tested, not assumed: we ran the document's own regeneration commands against the logs on disk.

YES
The 12 measured prefill rows regenerate cell-exact
MODEL=27b NODES="48 ... 55" bash sweep.sh --md reproduces the layer-6 table byte-for-byte from the logs. Every shape, tensor name and nrows=4 assertion matches.
NO
The entire 27B decode column has no logs anywhere
There is no sweep-gemv-27b/. MODE=gemv MODEL=27b bash sweep.sh --md prints MISSING for all 12 nodes. Every decode figure — the 2.24x/1.60x/3.54x/12.64x column, the 12-row per-node comparison, and the 73,356,044 cycles that anchor the "3.2x cheaper per token" result — is transcribed from a sibling document whose own logs are not in the tree. The numbers are internally consistent; they are simply unbacked.
NO
The layer-7 table cannot be produced by the command given for it
The documented command emits 4 rows and 15.02x; the published table has 7 rows and 17.65x. The three carried ffn_* rows are disclosed in prose after the table but carry no marker inside it — unlike the sibling document, which has a dedicated source column reading "inferred, = K53". Those three rows are 43% of the table and 62% of the layer's weights.
NO
Every aggregate row is typed by hand
sweep.sh --md never emits a LAYER row or a geometric mean, so no tool checks them. That is precisely how defect D1 got in and stayed in.
PART
Nothing is version-pinned
No commit, toolchain version, simulator build or model hash. The binaries were built from an uncommitted working tree and none can be rebuilt from branch HEAD. The logs record which binary ran — the single most useful field, and the one that surfaced the anomaly below — but no engine string, model path or timestamp.
PART
Repeatability is about ±0.6%, and cells are quoted to nine digits
The harness's own --selfcheck re-ran two legs and returned 823,397 against the published 818,314 (+0.62%) and 1,651,086 against 1,651,949 (−0.05%). No tolerance is stated anywhere, yet the document distinguishes 21.57x from 21.60x — a 0.14% difference, well inside the floor.
PART
One binary out of 48 is a different build — verified benign
bin-d4-k59 was built 2026-08-07 while its own column-mates were built 08-24; it is 104 bytes larger and carries a weights-in-HVM redirect from a different branch. Exactly one function differs semantically, it runs at model load outside the ROI, the redirect provably never fired, and both vd4dot kernels are instruction-for-instruction identical to the other eleven. Its number is not an outlier against the same-shape ssm_out. No published figure is suspect — but the A/B for that node is not same-vintage, and only disassembly established that it does not matter.
The correctness question — and why these logs cannot answer it

A speedup with no correctness gate is not a result, so we looked hard for one. The repo has the right tool: verify.sh runs pristine, prefetch and d4 in functional mode with greedy sampling and compares generated text, and q1_0_reproduce.md documents MODEL=27b bash verify.sh. It even records the subtlety that matters: d4 prefill is not bit-exact by construction, because the vd4dot GEMM folds the scale into each q8 group and accumulates four times per block, a different rounding order. Equal greedy text is the acceptance bar.

None of that reaches these numbers. No saved 27B verify.sh result exists anywhere in the tree. The logs cannot substitute: the ROI halts every run at the end of the bracketed matmul, so not one token was ever generated in any of the 104 logs — "The capital of France" in each is the echoed prompt. And every leg drew a different random sampler seed (sweep.sh passes no -s), so the comparison was foreclosed twice over.

Consequence: a silent numerical regression in the vd4dots prefill kernel would leave all 48 cycle counts and this entire document unchanged. The document does not mention correctness at all. One -s 1 in the sweep invocation would have made a four-way text comparison fall out of the measurement for free.

06 — ACTIONSWhat would close the gaps

Ranked by how much certainty each buys per unit of work. The first four cost minutes and no simulation.

  1. Fix the two layer-7 cells to 195,052,238 and 182,336,759.
  2. Make sweep.sh --md emit the LAYER rows and the geometric means. This is the one change that removes the class of error, not just the instance — no aggregate should be typed by a human again.
  3. Label the decode column. Either ship sweep-gemv-27b/, or state in the table that it is carried from profiling_gemv_27b.md with no logs in this tree.
  4. Add a source column to the layer-7 table, as the sibling document already does, and print layer 7's measured-only geometric mean (15.02x) beside the 17.65x blend.
  5. Delete the ZVFH sentence. Replace with: no RVV activation quantizer exists on RISC-V; writing one is the lever. Restate the 12.4x as 6.2x per token.
  6. Name the LM head. State that it is 4.96% of matmul weights, that 248320 % 64 == 0 passes by luck, and that the 4B and 8B heads fail the same gate — which is where 10.77x comes from.
  7. Publish the whole-model number, 20.8x. It is better than the headline, and it is the figure a reader actually wants.
  8. Pin the inputs — commit, toolchain, engine build, model sha256 — state a ±0.6% tolerance, and stop quoting cycle counts to nine significant digits.
  9. Add -s 1 to the sweep and save one MODEL=27b bash verify.sh run. That turns the correctness gate from "exists in the repo" into "was applied to these binaries".
  10. Disclose the two asymmetries: the one-time repack (break-even ~18–34 prompt tokens) and the upstream comparator's 32-of-128 lane utilization. Both make the work look better when stated honestly, because both currently work against it.

07 — APPENDIXMethod and limits

How this audit was conducted

Eleven independent auditors worked seven lenses — log reconciliation, harness fairness, arithmetic, source citations, reproducibility, selection bias, and simulator validity — each instructed to verify against primary evidence rather than the document's own words, and to report what checked out as well as what did not. Contested claims were then re-checked by separate agents. Every headline figure quoted in this opinion was independently recomputed by the lead auditor from the raw logs before publication.

No simulation was run: a single RTL leg costs up to 20 hours. The audit is therefore a check of the published numbers against the artifacts on disk, not a re-measurement.

Confirmed by direct inspection

  • The Setup table matches the elaborated RTL config exactly — NDS_VLEN 1024, NDS_NHART 1, ICACHE/DCACHE_SIZE_KB 32, L2C_CACHE_SIZE_KB 0, L3C_CACHE_SIZE_KB 2048.
  • The RVV_VLEN = 128 in every log is not a contradiction: the field is __riscv_vlenb(), which is bytes. 128 bytes = 1024 bits. The document is right and the log label is the misleading one.
  • 3.80 GB and 1.125 bits/weight both check out against the gguf; every weights cell equals ne0 × ne1; both layer weight totals are exact.
  • All six F/T curve fits reproduce to the digit from the 4B logs.

What this audit does not establish

  • That the kernels are numerically correct on this model. See section 05.
  • That the numbers transfer to silicon. Memory behind the L3 is idealised, and the comparator's lane utilization is VLEN-specific.
  • Any end-to-end speedup. The 20.8x covers MUL_MAT only; no measurement of non-MUL_MAT prefill work exists anywhere in the project.
  • Anything about the 512-token ubatch regime a real prefill runs. Everything measured here is a 4-token prompt.
Independent third-party opinion on profiling_gemm_27b.md, prepared 2026-09-02 from the artifacts in /home/nick/work/llama.cpp at branch q1_0-rvv-opt. Cycle counts quoted are the document's own; corrections are recomputed from the raw logs.

Independent verification · third-party opinion

Bonsai-27B Prefill Audit

Is profiling_gemm_27b.md a fair measurement, and can someone else reproduce it? Checked against the 48 raw simulator logs, the build and sweep scripts, the kernel source, the elaborated RTL config, and the 48 measurement binaries.

Subject profiling_gemm_27b.md, generated 2026-08-31 Audited 2026-09-02 Evidence 104 logs · 48 binaries · 8 scripts

01 — OPINIONVerdict

The measurement is fair. The four builds share one compile line and differ only in the three flags the document names; the "before" build is genuine upstream RVV code, not a straw man; the measured region is bracketed identically in both code paths; and all 48 legs ran once, in one pass, with no reruns. Every one of the 48 published cycle counts matches its log exactly, and every ratio, geometric mean and curve fit in the document reproduces. The residual bias that does exist runs against the author: the optimized builds pay a scalar activation quantizer that the baseline does not, so the published speedups are lower bounds, and the choice of geometric mean understates the model-wide result by 14%.

Reproducibility is partial. The 27B prefill half regenerates cell-exact from logs on disk. The 27B decode half — roughly half of every comparison the document makes — has no logs anywhere in the tree and no command that would produce them. Every aggregate row is typed by hand rather than emitted by the tool, and one of them is wrong by 23.6%. Nothing is version-pinned: no commit, no toolchain, no simulator build, no model hash, and the binaries were built from an uncommitted working tree.

A−
Fairness
Clean A/B, honest baseline, no selective reporting. Marked down for two undisclosed asymmetries, not for any rigged number.
C+
Reproducibility
Prefill tables regenerate exactly. Decode half unverifiable, aggregates hand-made, nothing pinned.
48/48
published cycle counts matched their log, to the digit
62
derived figures independently recomputed and confirmed
3
statements that are factually wrong
1
major evidence gap: the entire 27B decode column

02 — FAIRNESSWhich way does the bias point?

A speedup number can be flattered in a dozen quiet ways. Every one we tested for either was not there, or pushed the result down rather than up.

PASS
One compile line for all four builds
build.sh configures every variant with the same Release, -O3, -static, -march=rv64gv_zca_zcb_zcmp_zcmt_zicbop_zihintpause, ZVFH=OFF, OPENMP=OFF. Only GGML_CPU_REPACK, Q1_PREFETCH_DIST and GGML_RV_XANDESVDOT move, and only d4 appends _xandesvdot to the march string.
PASS
The baseline is real upstream, not a crippled build
GGML_CPU_REPACK=OFF removes nothing a Q1_0 tensor would otherwise get — the repack dispatcher has exactly one Q1_0 candidate, and llamafile sgemm (on in both arms) has no Q1_0 case at all. Pristine runs the vectorized ggml_vec_dot_q1_0_q8_0_vl256.
PASS
The measured region is the same region in both paths
The ROI opens at ggml-cpu.c:1744, before the extra-buffer dispatch, and closes after the compute on both branches — so each build counts its own activation quantization. The ANDESIM_ROI_CLEAR_DPREF experiment knob is absent from all 48 measurement binaries.
PASS
The optimizations physically executed
Disassembly finds 32 nds.vd4dots in each of the two d4 kernels and zero in the other three builds; in-kernel prefetch.r appears only in prefetch and d4. No silent fallback — which the repo's own check-vd4dots.sh notes has happened before.
PASS
No selective reporting
All 48 legs are fresh run lines in one pass, zero resumes, zero non-zero exits. The resume rule structurally cannot re-run a leg that already produced a number. The only retry anywhere in the evidence set re-ran two 4B pristine legs that timed out — i.e. it helped the "before".
BIAS−
The optimized builds pay an activation quantizer the baseline does not
Pristine quantizes activations with the RVV quantize_row_q8_0; all three repack builds run the pure-scalar ggml_quantize_mat_q8_0_4x1, with an out-of-line __roundf per element, inside the same ROI. That is 6–60% of every published d4 cycle count and under 0.5% of the matching pristine one. Equalize it and attn_v/attn_k go from 11.40x to roughly 24–29x. The published speedups are lower bounds.
BIAS−
The mean chosen is the conservative one
The geometric mean gives a 1024-row node the same vote as a 17408-row node. Cycle-weighted over the whole model the result is 20.8x, not the document's 18.15x. The harness even documents the choice: sweep.sh refuses to print a cycle-weighted ratio because it "reads like a per-node speedup without being one".
Two more checks, and the one bias that points the other way
BIAS−
Prefetch's 1.07x is a floor, not a ceiling
The core, caches and 2 MB L3 are Verilator-elaborated Andes RTL, but main memory behind the L3 is a flat 1-cycle TLM model (vsim_andesim/src/platform/simple_memory.hpp:40, unsigned latency = 1). The prefetch stage exists to hide miss latency and this machine has almost none to hide, so it is the one number that should grow on silicon. The document's own explanation of it appeals to latency the simulator does not model.
BIAS+
The upstream comparator uses 32 of the machine's 128 vector lanes
quants.c:493 pins the upstream kernel to vsetvl_e8m1(32) with a horizontal reduction every 32 elements. On VLEN 1024 the e8m1 VLMAX is 128, so 96 lanes idle. This is unmodified upstream and therefore the right "what does upstream get on this chip today" number — but a material share of 20.6x is a 32-lane algorithm on a 128-lane machine, and the same figure would be far smaller at VLEN 256. The repo documents this in a sibling file; this write-up neither states nor links it.
GAP
The one-time repack is excluded and never mentioned
The layout conversion runs at model load, outside the ROI, at roughly 18 scalar instructions per weight element — about 1.6–2.4 billion cycles for ffn_down, or 58–141x one measured matmul of the same tensor. Excluding it is legitimate: it is amortized, upstream does exactly the same through the same hook for q4_0/q4_K/q6_K, and break-even against upstream arrives after about 18–34 prompt tokens. But a reader is never told, and the ~3x model-load inflation is visible in the timestamps of the very logs shipped as evidence.

03 — SCALEWhat the evidence actually supports

The document never states a whole-model number. Built from its own per-node measurements, weighted by the real layer counts (48 SSM + 16 attention) and the LM head, it is higher than every headline the document does give.

Whole-model MUL_MAT, cycle-weighted497 nodes · 94.57 G → 4.55 G cycles · recomputed here
20.8×
Document's headlinegeometric mean over 10 optimizable nodes
18.15×
If the LM head had failed the 64-row gatethe case on Bonsai-4B and 8B — 151,669 rows, 151669 % 64 = 53
10.8×
0×10×20.8×

Bars are drawn to the same linear scale. The 20.8x figure is insensitive to how the LM head is charged — as a 4-token gemm, a 2-token gemv, a 1-token gemv, or omitted entirely, it spans only 20.33–20.76x. It still excludes all non-MUL_MAT work, so it is an upper bound on end-to-end prefill.

The gap from 18.15x decomposes cleanly: geometric to cycle-weighted over the same ten shapes is +13.3%, layer multiplicity +2.5%, including the un-repacked ssm_alpha/ssm_beta is −2.0%, and the LM head is +0.4%.

The third bar is the document's largest undisclosed risk. output.weight is [5120 × 248320] — 1.27 G weights, 4.96% of every matmul weight in the model, larger than three whole layers. It is MUL_MAT node #497 and was never measured. It clears the repack gate only because 248320 is divisible by 64. Had it failed, it would be 50.3% of the optimized budget and the model-wide result would drop to 10.77x. The document spends a paragraph on that exact sensitivity for two tensors worth 0.13% of a layer, and does not name the tensor where it matters 5,000 times more.

04 — DEFECTSWhat is actually wrong

Three statements are false and several are imprecise. None of them moves a measured cycle count; two of them move a published number, and one sends the reader after a fix that does not exist.

D1

The layer-7 LAYER row is wrong by 23.6% in two cells

Error

| | LAYER | | 372,244,480 | 1,380,604,045 | 241,152,929 | 225,336,152 | 66,024,863 |

True values: +repack is 195,052,238, not 241,152,929. +prefetch is 182,336,759, not 225,336,152. The other three cells in the same row are exact, and layer 6's equivalent row is correct in all four columns. The wrong values are not any subset-sum of the measured nodes, so they are stale, not an alternative aggregation.

Impact: no speedup, geometric mean or conclusion derives from this row — every ratio in the document is computed per node and all of them check out. But a reader who divides the row to sanity-check the layer gets 5.72x instead of the true 7.08x.

D2

The vector quantizer the document blames a build flag for does not exist

Error

Its vector twin is gated behind __riscv_zvfh, and the measurement build sets -DGGML_RV_ZVFH=OFF.

What is true: on RISC-V, arch-fallback.h:221 unconditionally aliases ggml_quantize_mat_q8_0_4x1_generic to ggml_quantize_mat_q8_0_4x1. Both arms of the #if defined(__riscv_zvfh) at repack.cpp:347-351 therefore call the same scalar function. There is no RISC-V vector implementation anywhere in the tree, and building with ZVFH=ON would change nothing.

Impact: no cycle count changes — prefill genuinely does run a scalar quantizer. What changes is the remedy. The document points the reader at a CMake option, implying the measurement handicapped itself and one flag recovers the loss. The real work is writing an RVV quantizer, which the author's own opt_roadmap.md correctly lists as unwritten code.

D3

Half of the 12.4x fixed-cost gap is just four tokens instead of two

Overstated

So decode gets a vector quantizer and prefill gets a scalar one. That is the whole 12.4x fixed-cost gap

What is true: 489,581/39,491 = 12.40x per call is correct, but the gemm call quantizes 4 token rows and the gemv call 2. Per token it is 122,395 vs 19,745 — 6.2x. The two Fs differ in routine and in workload; only the first is the scalar/vector choice.

Impact: the penalty attributed to the scalar quantizer halves. The conclusion survives — a 6.2x per-token penalty is still the largest single item in a small prefill matmul, and vectorizing it is still the best remaining prefill lever.

Four smaller inaccuracies, with corrections
D4
"F stays put" is contradicted by the table above it
gemv F goes 13,379 → 27,294 → 39,491 — a 2.95x rise the document prints itself. gemm F rises 23%. The point being made (F's share grows as T collapses) is true and worth making; the absolute claim is not.
D5
"0.06% of the layer's weights" — the true figure is 0.128%
The Notes bullet halves it, counting one tensor instead of two. Line 71 of the same document states it correctly as 0.12%. The companion figure in the same sentence, 2.7% of optimized cycles, is right (2.74%).
D6
"their four cycle counts agree to 0.3%" — only one of the two does
ssm_alpha's spread is 0.30%; ssm_beta's is 0.46%. Worth stating precisely, because these two tensors run bit-identical code in all four builds and are therefore the document's only measurement of its own noise floor.
D7
"Measuring one of each covers the whole model" — it omits the largest tensor
The LM head is 4.96% of all matmul weights and is measured nowhere. See section 03.

05 — REPRODUCTIONCan someone else get these numbers?

Tested, not assumed: we ran the document's own regeneration commands against the logs on disk.

YES
The 12 measured prefill rows regenerate cell-exact
MODEL=27b NODES="48 ... 55" bash sweep.sh --md reproduces the layer-6 table byte-for-byte from the logs. Every shape, tensor name and nrows=4 assertion matches.
NO
The entire 27B decode column has no logs anywhere
There is no sweep-gemv-27b/. MODE=gemv MODEL=27b bash sweep.sh --md prints MISSING for all 12 nodes. Every decode figure — the 2.24x/1.60x/3.54x/12.64x column, the 12-row per-node comparison, and the 73,356,044 cycles that anchor the "3.2x cheaper per token" result — is transcribed from a sibling document whose own logs are not in the tree. The numbers are internally consistent; they are simply unbacked.
NO
The layer-7 table cannot be produced by the command given for it
The documented command emits 4 rows and 15.02x; the published table has 7 rows and 17.65x. The three carried ffn_* rows are disclosed in prose after the table but carry no marker inside it — unlike the sibling document, which has a dedicated source column reading "inferred, = K53". Those three rows are 43% of the table and 62% of the layer's weights.
NO
Every aggregate row is typed by hand
sweep.sh --md never emits a LAYER row or a geometric mean, so no tool checks them. That is precisely how defect D1 got in and stayed in.
PART
Nothing is version-pinned
No commit, toolchain version, simulator build or model hash. The binaries were built from an uncommitted working tree and none can be rebuilt from branch HEAD. The logs record which binary ran — the single most useful field, and the one that surfaced the anomaly below — but no engine string, model path or timestamp.
PART
Repeatability is about ±0.6%, and cells are quoted to nine digits
The harness's own --selfcheck re-ran two legs and returned 823,397 against the published 818,314 (+0.62%) and 1,651,086 against 1,651,949 (−0.05%). No tolerance is stated anywhere, yet the document distinguishes 21.57x from 21.60x — a 0.14% difference, well inside the floor.
PART
One binary out of 48 is a different build — verified benign
bin-d4-k59 was built 2026-08-07 while its own column-mates were built 08-24; it is 104 bytes larger and carries a weights-in-HVM redirect from a different branch. Exactly one function differs semantically, it runs at model load outside the ROI, the redirect provably never fired, and both vd4dot kernels are instruction-for-instruction identical to the other eleven. Its number is not an outlier against the same-shape ssm_out. No published figure is suspect — but the A/B for that node is not same-vintage, and only disassembly established that it does not matter.
The correctness question — and why these logs cannot answer it

A speedup with no correctness gate is not a result, so we looked hard for one. The repo has the right tool: verify.sh runs pristine, prefetch and d4 in functional mode with greedy sampling and compares generated text, and q1_0_reproduce.md documents MODEL=27b bash verify.sh. It even records the subtlety that matters: d4 prefill is not bit-exact by construction, because the vd4dot GEMM folds the scale into each q8 group and accumulates four times per block, a different rounding order. Equal greedy text is the acceptance bar.

None of that reaches these numbers. No saved 27B verify.sh result exists anywhere in the tree. The logs cannot substitute: the ROI halts every run at the end of the bracketed matmul, so not one token was ever generated in any of the 104 logs — "The capital of France" in each is the echoed prompt. And every leg drew a different random sampler seed (sweep.sh passes no -s), so the comparison was foreclosed twice over.

Consequence: a silent numerical regression in the vd4dots prefill kernel would leave all 48 cycle counts and this entire document unchanged. The document does not mention correctness at all. One -s 1 in the sweep invocation would have made a four-way text comparison fall out of the measurement for free.

06 — ACTIONSWhat would close the gaps

Ranked by how much certainty each buys per unit of work. The first four cost minutes and no simulation.

  1. Fix the two layer-7 cells to 195,052,238 and 182,336,759.
  2. Make sweep.sh --md emit the LAYER rows and the geometric means. This is the one change that removes the class of error, not just the instance — no aggregate should be typed by a human again.
  3. Label the decode column. Either ship sweep-gemv-27b/, or state in the table that it is carried from profiling_gemv_27b.md with no logs in this tree.
  4. Add a source column to the layer-7 table, as the sibling document already does, and print layer 7's measured-only geometric mean (15.02x) beside the 17.65x blend.
  5. Delete the ZVFH sentence. Replace with: no RVV activation quantizer exists on RISC-V; writing one is the lever. Restate the 12.4x as 6.2x per token.
  6. Name the LM head. State that it is 4.96% of matmul weights, that 248320 % 64 == 0 passes by luck, and that the 4B and 8B heads fail the same gate — which is where 10.77x comes from.
  7. Publish the whole-model number, 20.8x. It is better than the headline, and it is the figure a reader actually wants.
  8. Pin the inputs — commit, toolchain, engine build, model sha256 — state a ±0.6% tolerance, and stop quoting cycle counts to nine significant digits.
  9. Add -s 1 to the sweep and save one MODEL=27b bash verify.sh run. That turns the correctness gate from "exists in the repo" into "was applied to these binaries".
  10. Disclose the two asymmetries: the one-time repack (break-even ~18–34 prompt tokens) and the upstream comparator's 32-of-128 lane utilization. Both make the work look better when stated honestly, because both currently work against it.

07 — APPENDIXMethod and limits

How this audit was conducted

Eleven independent auditors worked seven lenses — log reconciliation, harness fairness, arithmetic, source citations, reproducibility, selection bias, and simulator validity — each instructed to verify against primary evidence rather than the document's own words, and to report what checked out as well as what did not. Contested claims were then re-checked by separate agents. Every headline figure quoted in this opinion was independently recomputed by the lead auditor from the raw logs before publication.

No simulation was run: a single RTL leg costs up to 20 hours. The audit is therefore a check of the published numbers against the artifacts on disk, not a re-measurement.

Confirmed by direct inspection

  • The Setup table matches the elaborated RTL config exactly — NDS_VLEN 1024, NDS_NHART 1, ICACHE/DCACHE_SIZE_KB 32, L2C_CACHE_SIZE_KB 0, L3C_CACHE_SIZE_KB 2048.
  • The RVV_VLEN = 128 in every log is not a contradiction: the field is __riscv_vlenb(), which is bytes. 128 bytes = 1024 bits. The document is right and the log label is the misleading one.
  • 3.80 GB and 1.125 bits/weight both check out against the gguf; every weights cell equals ne0 × ne1; both layer weight totals are exact.
  • All six F/T curve fits reproduce to the digit from the 4B logs.

What this audit does not establish

  • That the kernels are numerically correct on this model. See section 05.
  • That the numbers transfer to silicon. Memory behind the L3 is idealised, and the comparator's lane utilization is VLEN-specific.
  • Any end-to-end speedup. The 20.8x covers MUL_MAT only; no measurement of non-MUL_MAT prefill work exists anywhere in the project.
  • Anything about the 512-token ubatch regime a real prefill runs. Everything measured here is a 4-token prompt.
Independent third-party opinion on profiling_gemm_27b.md, prepared 2026-09-02 from the artifacts in /home/nick/work/llama.cpp at branch q1_0-rvv-opt. Cycle counts quoted are the document's own; corrections are recomputed from the raw logs.

**Verdict: the measurement is fair; the reproducibility is only half there.**

Full audit opinion: https://claude.ai/code/artifact/23a8edb8-a9e7-43d7-bd60-9a4cd296794b

**Fairness — A−.** I checked every way this could be flattered, and found none:
- All four builds share **one** cmake line; only the 3 named flags differ.
- `pristine` is real upstream RVV (`ggml_vec_dot_q1_0_q8_0_vl256`), not a straw man. `GGML_CPU_REPACK=OFF` removes nothing else for Q1_0.
- The ROI bracket is identical in both code paths (`ggml-cpu.c:1744`).
- `nds.vd4dots` is really executed (32 per kernel, 0 in the other builds) — no silent fallback.
- All 48 legs ran once, in one pass, zero reruns. The only retry anywhere helped the *baseline*.

The biases that exist push the result **down**, not up:
- The optimized builds pay a scalar activation quantizer that pristine does not (6–60% of each `d4` number). Equalize it and `attn_v` goes 11.40x → ~24-29x. **The published speedups are lower bounds.**
- Geometric mean understates: whole-model cycle-weighted is **20.8x**, not 18.15x.

One bias points the other way, undisclosed: upstream uses **32 of the machine's 128 vector lanes** (`quants.c:493`), so part of 20.6x is VLEN-specific.

**Reproducibility — C+.** Three real problems:
1. **The layer-7 LAYER row is wrong by 23.6%** — `+repack` should be 195,052,238 (not 241,152,929), `+prefetch` 182,336,759 (not 225,336,152). No speedup derives from it, but it is published and bolded.
2. **The entire 27B decode column has no logs anywhere.** No `sweep-gemv-27b/`. That is half of every comparison in the doc.
3. **Every aggregate is typed by hand** — `--md` never emits a LAYER row or a geomean. That is exactly how #1 got in.

**Three statements are factually wrong.** The biggest: *"Its vector twin is gated behind `__riscv_zvfh`"* — `arch-fallback.h:221` aliases the generic scalar routine to the arch name on RISC-V, so **no vector twin exists** and `ZVFH=ON` changes nothing. The remedy the doc points at is a flag; the real work is writing an RVV quantizer.

**The undisclosed risk that matters most:** the LM head (`output.weight [5120 × 248320]`) is 4.96% of all matmul weights, was never measured, and passes the 64-row gate only because 248320 % 64 == 0. On 4B/8B (151,669 rows) it **fails** — and there the model-wide figure would be 10.77x instead of 20.76x.

**Not upheld:** the `bin-d4-k59` anomaly is real (built 08-07, +212 B `.text`) but **benign** — the one differing function runs at model load outside the ROI and both vd4dot kernels are instruction-identical. No published figure is suspect.
